coredata.dc:description: Bisphenols are often detected in environmental samples and are implicated as endocrine-disrupting compounds. This study examines the photodegradation of bisphenol S (BPS), a common replacement of bisphenol A, using a solar-activated persulfate (solar/PS) system at batch and pilot scale. The photodegradation of BPS followed pseudo-first-order decay; the observed kinetic constant increased with oxidant concentration up to 0.19 min−1 at 500 μg L−1 and decreased as the initial BPS concentration increased (0.0091 min−1 at 3 mg L−1). The system's efficiency was approximately three times lower under alkaline conditions, while the apparent kinetic constant significantly decreased in secondary effluent. Interestingly, complete BPS removal was achieved in the pilot reactor under natural sunlight at approximately 20 kJ L−1. Based on scavenging experiments and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, the degradation was driven by the synergistic action of sulfate radicals (SO4 • -), singlet oxygen (1O2), and hydroxyl radicals (HO•). Five transformation products (TPs) were identified by LC/TOF-MS, and a plausible pathway is proposed. According to the ECOSAR model, some TPs exhibited higher predicted toxicity than the parent compound for certain indicators, suggesting the need for longer treatment times or more intensive conditions. Seed-based assays showed inhibition by BPS alone, while solar/PS treatment generally attenuated the toxicity of the mixture of BPS and TPs. Nevertheless, residual, time-dependent inhibition persisted in some species, underscoring species-specific risks and the need for multi-bioassay evaluation before reuse.

ce:section.ce:para: Several natural and synthetic compounds have been found to induce adverse effects in living organisms. Among them, the family of endocrine disrupting compounds (EDCs) has received significant attention due to their potential to disrupt reproductive and metabolic processes and affect endocrine and immune systems (Bolong et al., 2009; Kolatorova et al., 2018; Potakis et al., 2017). Within this group, bisphenols are the most representative members. They are mainly used in the manufacture of plastics and serve as additives in flame retardants, thermal papers, and brake fluids. Bisphenols are a group of chemical compounds characterized by two phenol functional groups. The best-known substance in this class is bisphenol A (4,4′-(propane-2,2-diyl) diphenol, BPA). BPA is used in the production of polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins, which are commonly found in food and beverage containers, medical devices, and dental sealants (Sharma et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2020). BPA can leach from containers into food and beverages, prompting a shift to bisphenol S (4,4′-sulfonylbisphenol; BPS) (Kim et al., 2020). However, studies suggest BPS may have similar health concerns to BPA, leading to its classification as a regrettable substitution in some applications (Gayrard et al., 2019). Despite growing concern, BPS production has been increasing and may surpass BPA as regulatory restrictions increase.

These substances enter aquatic habitats via the discharge from sewage treatment facilities, industrial emissions, and agricultural drainage (Rodríguez et al., 2007). The extensive usage over a long period results in the accumulation of these substances, both on the surface and underground, along with their derivatives (Kim et al., 2020). Although they are detected at low levels (ng/L to μg/L), they exhibit potent toxicological effects (He et al., 2014; Potakis et al., 2017). Reports of bisphenol contamination originating from plastics have been emerging since 2007, attracting widespread attention (Fang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024; Tasnesem et al., 2025). The regulation of bisphenols continues to be an issue of scientific research and public concern. They challenge conventional treatment because of low ambient concentrations and structural complexity. To address this need, advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) have emerged as a promising solution for the degradation of persistent micropollutants. AOPs are physicochemical water treatment techniques that degrade pollutants and remediate contaminated water (Oturan and Aaron, 2014). Their function is based on the activation of oxidant precursors with low oxidative capacity to produce highly reactive species for the oxidation of pollutants. These reactive species react with various classes of organic compounds, leading to the production of simpler organic compounds or complete mineralization to carbon dioxide, water, and other harmless substances. In the literature, the most common oxidant used, for the production of hydroxyl radicals (

(E0 = 2.60 V). Although peroxymonosulfate (PMS) is also a common oxidant capable of generating sulfate radicals, PS was selected for this study. PS is generally preferred for large-scale applications due to its higher stability, lower cost, and solid state at room temperature, which simplifies storage and transportation logistics compared to liquid peroxide precursors or hygroscopic PMS salts (Malefane et al., 2024).

A number of techniques have been used to successfully activate oxidant species precursors for radical production, such as exposure to UV irradiation (Gao et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2017), thermal/heat activation (Chen et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2015; Lalas et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2013a), adjustment of initial pH (Boczkaj and Fernandes, 2017), ultrasound (Arvaniti et al., 2020; Campbell and Hoffmann, 2015) and transition metals (Dong et al., 2019; Lalas et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2013).

For homogeneous AOPs, irradiation from various light sources has been used to generate radicals and eliminate a wide range of organic pollutants from wastewater (Lalas et al., 2025). Light activation decomposes PS into two

. These processes offer high degradation efficiencies and mild reaction conditions (Huang et al., 2017; Saien et al., 2015; Ye et al., 2016). In addition, homogeneous processes avoid mass transfer limitations and the challenges associated with heterogeneous catalysts, including complex production processes, difficult catalyst recovery, and potential environmental pollution from leached metal ions (Santiago-Espiñeira et al., 2025; Calaixo et al., 2023; Durán et al., 2022), Furthermore, while heterogeneous catalysts and semiconductor nanomaterials offer alternative activation routes, they often suffer from deactivation and the technical challenge of separating the catalyst from the treated effluent (Malefane et al., 2024). Solar light activation represents a sustainable, energy-efficient approach that circumvents these separation issues and avoids the high operational costs associated with artificial UVC lamp. While direct photolysis can contribute to the removal of pollutants, its efficiency is often limited and governed by the pollutant's light absorption properties and the system's operating conditions.

The predominant light source in the literature for the activation of the oxidants is UV irradiation of 254 nm. However, the implementation of these techniques, especially on a large scale, seems to be limited due to the high costs involved (Tan et al., 2021). For these reasons, in recent years the use of solar light in heterogeneous and homogeneous systems is of great scientific interest. Solar technologies have been studied and developed more extensively as they have proven that they can successfully implement a green approach to dealing with micropollutants, both on a laboratory and pilot scale (Malato et al., 2009; Solís et al., 2019; Stathoulopoulos et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2021).

BPS has been treated by Cu3P/biochar/PS (Ioannidi et al., 2024a), photocatalysis (Rong et al., 2024), sonolysis (Nejumal et al., 2024), UVC/NaClO (Shah et al., 2025), UVC/PS (Shah et al., 2025), UVC/H2O2 (Shah et al., 2025), and solar/Na2CO3/PMS.

To our knowledge, this study is the first to investigate BPS degradation by a pilot-scale unit using real sunlight to activate sodium persulfate. It is also the first to examine the transformation pathway of BPS under solar/PS treatment and simultaneously evaluate both the ecotoxicity of the byproducts using QSAR models and the phytotoxicity of the treated samples from the examined solar/PS/BPS system. While previous studies provide valuable insights, there remains a critical gap in the demonstration of the process under realistic (pilot-scale) solar conditions and the comprehensive evaluation of the ecotoxicological profile of the transformation products.

Thus, the present study aims to investigate the degradation of BPS using solar radiation to activate persulfate, comprising both laboratory and pilot-scale experiments. Firstly, in the batch laboratory reactor under simulated solar irradiation, the effects of initial concentrations of both the oxidant and BPS were examined, followed by the influence of pH and the reaction mechanism, using appropriate radical scavengers and Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy. TPs were identified, and a degradation pathway was proposed. The ecotoxicity of the TPs was assessed, along with the overall phytotoxicity of the treated samples. Finally, the effects of synthetic and real water matrices were investigated at both laboratory and pilot scale using a stainless steel (SS) photoreactor equipped with a flat plate reflector (FPR) under natural solar irradiation. Selected parameters were studied to assess the potential of the system for real applications.

Sodium persulfate (SPS, Na2S2O8, ≥98 %, CAS: 7775-27-1) was acquired from Scharlau (Spain). Bis(4-hydroxyphenyl) sulfone or bisphenol-S (C12H10O4S, ≥99 %, CAS: 80-09-1) was purchased from Alfa Aesar (Germany). Sodium chloride (NaCl, ≥99 %, CAS: 7647-14-5), sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3, ≥99 %, CAS: 144-55-8), sodium nitrate (NaNO3, ≥99 %, CAS: 7631-99-4), humic acid (≥98 %, CAS: 1415-93-6), tert-butyl alcohol (tert-butanol, (CH3)3COH, ≥99,5 %, CAS: 75-65-0) were supplied by Sigma-Aldrich. Methanol (CH3OH, ≥99 %, CAS: 67-56-1) was purchased from Fisher Chemical, and sodium azide (NaN3, CAS: 26,628-22-8) was supplied by Merck KGaA (Germany). For pH regulation, sodium hydroxide (NaOH, ≥99 %, CAS: 1310-73-2) and sulfuric acid (H2SO4, CAS: 7664-93-9) were also purchased from the same supplier. For HPLC analysis, acetonitrile (CH3CN, CAS: 75-05-8) was purchased by Carlo Erba (France) and phosphoric acid (H3PO4, CAS: 7664-38-2) by Sigma-Aldrich (Switzerland). All chemicals were used as received without further purification.

Most of the experiments were carried out with ultrapure water (UPW) solutions produced by a Millipore water purification system with a resistivity of 18.2 MΩ cm at 25 °C. Experiments were conducted using real water matrices such as commercially bottled water (BW), and secondary wastewater effluent from the treatment plant of the University of Patras campus, before chlorination (WW). These samples were subjected to filtration with a 0.45 μm nylon membrane to remove particles. Deionized water for pilot experiments was produced by a lab-scale system (Watera Hellas). Additional physicochemical data are given in Table 1 .

The laboratory-scale BPS degradation experiments were carried out in a beaker reactor of a total volume of 150 mL, open to the atmosphere. A BPS stock solution in UPW was prepared. The reactor was brought to 100 mL with the target matrix and spiked to the desired BPS concentration ([BPS]). The experiment was initiated upon simultaneous addition of PS and activation of the lamp. The solution was continuously stirred with a magnetic stirrer throughout the experiment. Samples of 1.2 mL were withdrawn at certain intervals, quenched with methanol (0.3 mL), filtered (0.22 μm PVDF), and analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (Waters Alliance 2695 HPLC). The radiation source was a solar simulator, Oriel LCS-100, with a 100 W xenon (ozone free) lamp equipped with an AM 1.5G filter at an emitted light intensity of 7.3 × 10−7 photons L−1 s−1, as determined by actinometry (Ioannidou et al., 2016) and the distance between the lamp and the reactor was 20 cm. The experiments were conducted at ambient temperature; monitoring indicated that temperature variation was negligible (<2 °C) throughout the reaction Experiments were run in duplicate (relative deviation <6 %); results are reported as means.

The oxidation system was transferred to a pilot plant to evaluate the system's efficiency under more realistic conditions. Experiments were performed in a stainless-steel flat plate reflector consisting of seven borosilicate tubes mounted on a fixed platform with a 45° inclination, together with a tank and a centrifugal pump. Each tube had an outer diameter of 32 mm and a length of 1.5 m (Kouvelis et al., 2023). A detailed schematic representation of the experimental setup is provided in Fig. 1 . The reactor consists of seven borosilicate glass tubes arranged in parallel, mounted on a fixed platform. The photoreactor was located at the Department of Chemical Engineering (University of Patras, Greece). The total volume (VT) was 35 L, and the total irradiated area was approximately 1.1 m2, with the irradiated volume (Vi) being approximately 7.9 L (Ioannidi et al., 2023). At the beginning of the process, BPS solution (500 μg L−1) was introduced into the tank where it was continuously stirred using aeration and entered the reactor with the flow provided by the centrifugal pump. The flow rate was maintained at 12 L min−1 using a centrifugal pump operating at a fixed valve position, which was calibrated volumetrically prior to the experiments (measuring volume over time) to ensure constant hydraulic conditions. After complete mixing of the matrix and contaminant solution, the desired amount of oxidant was introduced into the tank, and the experiment started. As before, 1.2 mL sample extractions were taken at specific intervals, and a similar procedure was followed.

ce:section.ce:section-title: High performance liquid chromatography and transformation products identification
ce:section.ce:para: To monitor BPS concentrations, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC; Waters Alliance 2695) was used. Chromatographic conditions (mobile phase, flow rate, injection volume) followed Ioannidi et al. (2024a). Identification of transformation products (TPs) formed during the solar/PS process was performed by liquid chromatography–time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LC–TOF-MS). The analytical methodology is provided in the Supplementary Information and in Ioannidi et al. (2024a).

The identification of the reactive species produced by the studied system was performed using electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy. A JEOL X310 spectrometer equipped with an LC12 aqueous flat cell was used. 5,5-Dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO, 100 mM; CAS 3317-61-1) and 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine (TEMP, 1 mM; CAS 768-66-1) served as spin traps for sulfate/hydroxyl radicals and singlet oxygen, respectively. The microwave power was set to 10 mW after preliminary experiments to prevent saturation, and the sample volume was 100 μL. The experiments were performed at 25 °C. At least 5 scans were recorded, and the mean data are reported.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Prediction of ecotoxicity of transformation products using ECOSAR
ce:section.ce:para: QSAR models can predict the toxic effects of organic compounds by linking their chemical properties and molecular structure. Among the various prediction tools available, QSAR models are widely considered among the most reliable for evaluating aquatic toxicity, with their performance validated by comparing predicted baseline toxicity values to experimental data (Pore et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2020). In this study, ECOSAR (Version 2.2) developed by the USEPA was employed to assess the toxicity of BPS and its degradation products toward aquatic organisms such as daphnia, fish, and green algae. Table 2 summarizes toxicity categories.

Phytotoxicity tests evaluate the harmful effects of substances on plant growth and development. In the present study, three kinds of seeds were used: Sorghum saccharatum (Sorgho), the dicotyls Lepidium sativum (garden cress), and Brassica nigra (black mustard) to assess the phytotoxicity of the TPs. Specifically, treated samples prepared in UPW, containing initial concentrations of 3 mg L −1 BPS and 250 mg L −1 PS, were tested using the method described by Mendes et al. (2021). For each test, 5 mL of the treated sample were applied to a 90 mm diameter Petri dish containing 10 seeds placed on filter paper. UPW was used in the control setup, which showed a 100 % germination rate. Seeds were incubated at 25 °C in the dark for 72 h. Samples for the phytotoxicity assay were collected at 0, 30, 60, 120, 180, and 240 min, with each time point tested in triplicates. The experimental procedure followed ISO Standard 18,763.

ce:section.ce:section-title: The efficiency of solar alone & PS alone systems and their combination
ce:section.ce:para: As illustrated in Fig. 2 (a), the photolysis of the pollutant under simulated solar radiation ([PS]0 = 0 mg L −1 ) resulted in minimal removal (less than 5 % after 120 min). Similarly, the degradation of BPS by PS in the absence of light was negligible. These trends are reflected in the apparent kinetic constants kapp presented in Fig. 2(b), which were practically zero for both photolysis and dark PS treatments. Thus, BPS did not hydrolyze in the dark, and PS alone was inactive under these conditions. However, the simultaneous presence of both resulted in high removal levels, eliminating the targeted pollutant in less than 60 min. The synergistic effect was confirmed by a dramatic increase in the reaction rate, reaching a kapp value of 0.058 min−1, thereby validating the efficient activation of persulfate by solar light.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of the initial PS concentration
ce:section.ce:para: The initial PS concentration, [PS]0, was varied from 100 to 500 mg L−1. The initial BPS concentration, [BPS]0, was set at 0.5 mg L−1 to enable robust kinetics while remaining environmentally relevant (ng L−1–μg L−1). The collected results are shown in Fig. 2(c). With the addition of 125 mg L −1 of the oxidant, complete removal of BPS was achieved in 120 min. As can be seen, with increasing [PS]0, the time required for complete removal decreased to 60 and 30 min at initial concentrations of 250 and 500 mg L −1 , respectively. The results are confirmed by the calculated apparent kinetic constants (kapp) listed in Fig. 2(d), whose values increase with increasing [PS]0. This is attributed to the increased generation of reactive species at higher oxidant concentration. Nevertheless, excessive doses of PS may result in various drawbacks such as the reduction of the oxidation efficiency of the system due to the self-scavenging and the accumulation of sulfate ions in the receiving waters, which at high concentrations can be considered as pollutants (Chen et al., 2017). Therefore, to avoid the above and to reduce the costs of the process, the experimental procedure was continued with [PS]0 = 250 mg L−1.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of the initial bisphenol S concentration
ce:section.ce:para: Because environmental levels vary, [BPS]0 = 0.25–3 mg L−1 was investigated. The kinetics are shown in Fig. 2(e) and revealed that the system's degradation efficiency decreased at higher initial BPS concentrations. In fact, this decrease was proportional to the concentration selected, i.e. the more the initial concentration increased, the lower the kapp (Fig. 2(f)). To corroborate the indirect evidence from the scavenging experiments, the reactive species were directly identified using electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy (Fig. 5 ). The resulting spectra confirmed the presence of all three implicated oxidants: DMPO spin trapping revealed signals for both sulfate and hydroxyl radicals (Fig. 5(a)), while the characteristic triplet TEMPO signal confirmed the formation of singlet oxygen (Fig. 5(b)).

In a subsequent stage, the efficacy of the process was investigated in a pilot plant using solar irradiation to assess the path towards industrial implementation and scale-up. The characteristics of the pilot unit are described in detail in Section 2.3.2. The selection of the reactor type was informed by the pioneering study conducted by (Gomes et al., 2018). The researchers examined several pilot photoreactors made of different materials, also considering their durability and manufacturing process. The stainless-steel (SS) reactors demonstrated a high tube-to-area ratio; therefore, according to the researchers, SS reactors can be economically competitive under certain conditions compared to costly reflective materials or complex geometries that characterize compound parabolic concentrator photoreactors. The pilot-plant test investigated the photodegradation of 500 μg L−1 BPS using 250 mg L−1 PS in various aqueous matrices, such as deionized water (DW), commercially bottled water (BW), wastewater (WW), and in the presence of humic acid (HA). In addition, solar photolysis in the pilot-scale photoreactor was assessed.

From Fig. 6 , it is evident that for deionized water, bottled water, and humic acid, BPS was eliminated in less than 20 kJ L−1, while in the case of the secondary effluent, complete BPS removal was achieved under 50 kJ L−1. Photolysis was limited to almost 10 % after 20 kJ L−1, confirming the high retention time of bisphenols in environmental systems. Furthermore, given that the solution temperature increased to a maximum of 41 °C due to solar heating, a dark control experiment was conducted to rule out thermal activation. Heating the solution to 41 °C in the presence of persulfate resulted in minimal removal (<9 %), confirming that the degradation was primarily driven by photo-activation rather than thermal effects.

Notably, the inhibition observed in the presence of humic acid at pilot scale was milder than in the batch tests. This behaviour is explained by (i) reactor optics and hydrodynamics and (ii) the contribution from a different irradiance field. Indeed, the SS-FPR used is characterized by a short optical path in the borosilicate tubes while at the same time maintaining a high illuminated surface-to-volume ratio with a reflector. Consequently, despite the shading/masking by HA or secondary effluent, a larger number of incident photons reach persulfate, leading to higher production of reactive species. In addition, the high recirculation rate used in the pilot plant continuously renews the boundary layer at the irradiated wall, avoiding oxidant depletion near this layer and sustaining the steady-state formation of the reactive species, since the persulfate was in excess. During the experiments under sunlight, differences in the instantaneous UV and the broader spectral distribution compared to the solar simulator used in the bench experiments can also assist the production of radicals. This enhancement can lead to faster photodecomposition of humic acid or natural organic matter in the case of secondary effluent, further mitigating the dual role of organic matter as a masking agent and scavenger. Summarizing, the examined pilot plant, under the conditions in question, can work under more intensive conditions, thus decreasing the impact of the water matrix.

Our results are in accordance with the study by Wang et al. (2017) who investigated the degradation of BPS by heat activated persulfate and found that dimerization was one of the main routes. In general, coupling reactions of free radicals is a common transformation pathway during the treatment of pollutants bearing the phenolic ring by different persulfate-based processes (Ioannidi et al., 2024a, 2024b; Potakis et al., 2017; Frontistis et al., 2017; Outsiou et al., 2017).

The second pathway involves the opening of one of the two aromatic rings of BPS and the formation of two TPs (TP3 and TP4) with lower molecular weight than the target pollutant. Coha et al. (2020) studied the photocatalytic oxidation of BPS and found that ring cleavage is a significant transformation pathway. The last pathway includes the detachment of one of the two aromatic rings of BPS and can be attributed to the 4-phenolsulphonic acid (TP5) that was also detected in a previous study (Coha et al., 2021). Finally, these TPs can be transformed into aliphatic intermediates by further oxidation before complete mineralization.

In general, the studied sulfate radical-based advanced oxidation process (solar/PS) involves the activation of PS by UV irradiation and the formation of

· −
(Ioannidi et al., 2018; Antonopoulou, 2024). Moreover, after their formation

Based on ECOSAR data and applying the most conservative estimates for acute and chronic toxicity, the TPs of BPS exhibit a range of ecotoxicological effects on fish, Daphnia, and green algae. As ECOSAR predicts toxicity based on various chemical functional groups, several TPs were found to be more hazardous than the parent compound (Table 4 ). Specifically, TP1 and TP2 showed similar toxicity profiles, being acutely toxic to fish and green algae, and chronically very toxic to green algae, with Chronic Values (ChV) of 0.745 and 0.714 mg L −1 , respectively. While TP3 and TP4 were generally less acutely toxic, they demonstrated considerable chronic toxicity, being classified as very toxic and toxic to Daphnia and green algae, respectively.

Most notably, TP5 was predicted to be non harmful to all tested species, suggesting that if the solar/PS process is carried out for a sufficient duration, it can lead to the formation of non-toxic TPs.

These findings are in agreement with the literature, For example Shah et al. (2025) studied various processes (UVC/H2O2, UVC/persulfate, and UVC/NaClO) to evaluate the toxicity of BPS and its TPs and reported inhibition in Vibrio fischeri bioassays during the course of each treatment, except in the case of UVC/NaClO, where a slight reduction in inhibition was observed. In the case of UVC/persulfate, as also predicted in the present study, a higher inhibition in Vibrio fischeri was observed during the first 30 min of treatment, followed by a reduction to levels comparable with BPS. This indicates that initially more toxic products are formed and later degraded. It is important to note that the LC50, EC50, and ChV values are much higher than the environmental concentrations expected for these compounds, as BPS has been detected in the ng/L to μg L−1 range in aquatic environments. Therefore, the application of the solar/PS process for degrading BPS at environmental concentrations appears to be an effective option for water treatment, particularly considering the endocrine disrupting effects of BPS on animals and humans even at ng/L to μg L−1 levels (Wu et al., 2025; Mohan et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2019).

Considering that ECOSAR is a highly useful tool for predicting the toxicity of individual molecules, and given the importance of water conservation and reusability, the phytotoxic effects of the overall mixture of BPS and its TPs formed during the process were examined. For this purpose, three different seed species (Sorghum saccharatum, Lepidium sativum, and Brassica nigra) were used.

As can be seen in Fig. 8 , different plant species exhibit varying sensitivities to BPS and TPs. In all cases, BPS had an inhibitory effect on root and shoot growth, as well as on germination rate, compared to the controls (UPW only). Regarding germination, it was noticed that only Brassica nigra seeds were generally unaffected by the treated samples. BPS consistently inhibited root and shoot growth compared to the controls, except in the case of Brassica nigra shoot growth, where a slight stimulatory effect was observed (indicated by negative inhibition values in Fig. 8D). Additionally, the phytotoxicity of the treated samples was observed to vary significantly throughout the solar/PS process.

Nonetheless, a pronounced phytotoxic effect on both root and shoot growth was observed in Sorghum saccharatum and Brassica nigra, as shown in Fig. 8 (B, C, D). The highest root and shoot inhibition for Sorghum saccharatum was recorded after 120 min of treatment, at 50 % and 46 %, respectively. For Brassica nigra, root inhibition was observed at 120 and 240 min of treatment (36 % and 38 %, respectively), while shoot inhibition reached 50 % after 60 min of treatment. In contrast, Lepidium sativum showed a reduction in phytotoxic effects, with all treated samples being notably less phytotoxic compared to BPS alone, indicating greater tolerance to the mixture of BPS and its TPs.

The phytotoxicity bioassay conducted in this study provides a valuable preliminary assessment of the treated wastewater quality following the solar-activated persulfate oxidation of BPS. The results highlight the importance of evaluating the biological activity of both BPS and its TPs after advanced treatment, particularly when the treated effluent is intended for reuse. Although the sulfate radical-based oxidation process appears effective in reducing phytotoxicity; especially evident in Lepidium sativum, where all treated samples exhibited lower toxicity than the parent compound, caution is warranted. The observed variability among species, such as persistent inhibition in Sorghum saccharatum and Brassica nigra, suggests that conclusions about the overall biological safety of BPS degradation products cannot be drawn solely from a single bioassay.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Comparison with existing BPS degradation studies
ce:section.ce:para: To position the present solar driven persulfate process within the broader landscape of BPS remediation, Table 5 benchmarks representative persulfate based processes in terms of removal efficiency and kinetics, pH, qualitative operational energy burden, and the most plausible application context. Across the literature, a consistent trade off emerges between kinetic performance and energy sustainability. Systems activated by auxiliary energy inputs, including thermal activation and UV irradiation, can achieve rapid degradation and high apparent kinetic constants (kobs up to approximately 0.39 min−1 in UV/PS). However, they require continuous energy supply for heating or UV lamps. This operational requirement increases cost and carbon emissions when large treated volumes are targeted, and it tends to confine these options to controlled, compact implementations where electrical infrastructure and high process intensity are acceptable, such as point of use polishing in low turbidity waters or niche industrial applications where heating is feasible as shown in Table 5. Ultrasound activated persulfate may also provide fast kinetics (kobs up to 0.113 min−1) and can be less sensitive to optical limitations in turbid media; however, the very high electrical demand of transducers and dedicated equipment typically restricts its practicality to specialized, relatively low volume cases.

On the other hand, the solar assisted oxidation routes reduce the need for continuous electrical input during operation, but they shift the feasibility constraints toward footprint, residence time, and irradiance variability. In this context, the solar carbonate PMS system reported by Yuan et al. exhibits broad pH tolerance (pH 5.02 to 10.96) and strong performance under alkaline or carbonate rich conditions, supporting the relevance of non radical pathways when matrix composition favors such routes (Table 5). Catalytic persulfate activation using tailored biochars can also deliver high removal within short times in ultrapure water, but overall performance and robustness depend on catalyst preparation, handling and recovery, and are frequently diminished in real matrices due to scavenging and competitive reactions. Accordingly, the embedded energy and operational complexity associated with catalyst synthesis and management should be considered alongside apparent kinetics (Table 5).

Within the above framework, the Solar/PS process validated here at pilot scale represents a balanced option for tertiary polishing. Although the apparent kinetics are moderate relative to electricity driven activation, complete BPS removal was achieved in the 35 L pilot reactor under natural sunlight with low accumulated solar energy per treated volume, approximately 20 kJ L−1 in deionized water and below 50 kJ L−1 in secondary effluent (Table 5). These findings, together with the observed attenuation of phytotoxicity, support the relevance of solar driven persulfate activation for reuse oriented polishing where low operational electricity is prioritized. At the same time, it is important noting that the process should not be interpreted as universally superior. Practical deployment remains conditioned by the need for mildly acidic operation for optimal performance, management of sulfate residuals, irradiance driven variability, and the collector footprint and hydraulic residence time required for solar photoreactors, as well as capital cost. Therefore, the strength of the present approach lies in low energy tertiary treatment under favorable solar and space conditions, rather than in replacing compact electrically driven systems in all settings.

This study demonstrated that the solar/PS effectively eliminated BPS under both artificial and real sunlight. The photodegradation was well described by a pseudo-first-order model, and the increase in persulfate dose accelerated the degradation, while the apparent kinetic constant decreased at higher BPS concentrations. Interestingly, the photolysis or direct oxidation by persulfate indicated a large half-life of BPS in the environment. Water chemistry significantly influences the process efficiency: alkaline conditions slowed the removal, while the matrix constituents in environmentally relevant matrices, such as the secondary effluent, further decrease process efficiency. According to the mechanistic investigation, degradation proceeds via a dual-pathway mechanism, co-driven by the simultaneous action of sulfate and hydroxyl radicals and non-radical singlet oxygen. Five TPs were revealed using LC/TOF-MS, and a possible pathway that involves dimerization, and ring-cleavage/detachment steps was proposed. According to both theoretical QSAR models and phytotoxicity experiments, although toxicity in general decreased with irradiation time, some TPs can be more hazardous than BPS, highlighting the need for careful process optimisation to ensure degradation proceeds to non-toxic by-products. Interestingly, the pilot-scale implementation of the proposed system under natural sunlight validated the encouraging results of the batch-scale experiments.

Solar/PS appears to be a promising technology for the polishing of environmentally relevant samples; however, the optimisation of operating conditions is not solely a function of BPS removal; water chemistry and toxicological outcomes must also be integrated to determine optimal operating conditions. Furthermore, future work must also focus on the simultaneous efficiency of the examined system for disinfection to assess if the examined green system can be used as an integrated polishing step replacing well-known disinfectants.
